label: Clock tree objectives
lesson:
# Clock tree objectives

Clock tree synthesis (CTS) turns one clock net with thousands of sinks into a buffered network that delivers every edge on time. It runs after placement, when the flop locations are known, and before signal routing. A CTS engine is judged on a small set of numbers: latency, skew, slew and power. A tool designer needs these definitions exactly, because every algorithm in this domain optimises one of them while bounding the others, and static timing then consumes the result.

## Latency and insertion delay

The **latency** (insertion delay) of a sink is the time from the clock source to that sink's clock pin. It has two parts: the **source latency**, from the clock's origin (a PLL or a port) to the root of the tree, and the **network latency**, the sum of every buffer and wire delay along the tree path. For example, a source latency of 90 ps followed by buffers of 39, 62, 58 and 67 ps and a last wire of 10 ps gives a latency of $90 + 39 + 62 + 58 + 67 + 10 = 326$ ps. Latency itself does not appear in a setup check, because launch and capture both carry it, but large latency is costly: every stage burns power and adds on-chip variation that is not shared between branches.

## Global skew

**Skew** between two sinks is the difference of their latencies. The **global skew** of a tree is the largest latency minus the smallest over all sinks: for latencies 407, 405, 418, 386, 381 and 457 ps it is $457 - 381 = 76$ ps. Global skew is the number most CTS engines report and target, because it is cheap to compute and bounds every pairwise difference. Positive skew from launch to capture gives setup more time and takes the same amount from hold; this is the link to static timing, where skew enters each check directly.

## Local skew and why it matters more

Only flops joined by a timing path care about each other's clock. **Local skew** is the largest latency difference over sequentially adjacent pairs. If flops D, B and A are related by paths D to A, B to A and A to D, with latencies $A = 436$, $B = 445$, $D = 425$ ps, the local skew is $\max(11, 9, 11) = 11$ ps, while the global skew over a larger set might be 34 ps. A tree can therefore have large global skew and still be excellent, if unrelated sinks are the ones that differ. Useful-skew optimisation goes further and makes some local skews deliberately non-zero. A CTS engine that only minimises global skew may waste buffers equalising sinks that never talk to each other.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), the chapter on clock tree synthesis; Friedman, "Clock distribution networks in synchronous digital integrated circuits", Proceedings of the IEEE (2001).

problems.q: A clock leaves its source with 40 ps of source latency. On its way to flop FF7 it passes 4 buffers with delays 28, 38, 70, 48 ps, and the last wire to the clock pin adds 13 ps. What is the clock latency (insertion delay) at FF7, in ps?
problems.e: Latency is the sum of everything from the source to the clock pin: 40 + 28 + 38 + 70 + 48 + 13 = 237 ps.

problems.q: A clock leaves its source with 80 ps of source latency. On its way to flop FF7 it passes 5 buffers with delays 56, 40, 67, 64, 49 ps, and the last wire to the clock pin adds 15 ps. What is the clock latency (insertion delay) at FF7, in ps?
problems.e: Latency is the sum of everything from the source to the clock pin: 80 + 56 + 40 + 67 + 64 + 49 + 15 = 371 ps.

problems.q: A clock leaves its source with 90 ps of source latency. On its way to flop FF7 it passes 4 buffers with delays 58, 55, 43, 55 ps, and the last wire to the clock pin adds 7 ps. What is the clock latency (insertion delay) at FF7, in ps?
problems.e: Latency is the sum of everything from the source to the clock pin: 90 + 58 + 55 + 43 + 55 + 7 = 308 ps.

problems.q: After CTS, the 5 clock sinks of a block report latencies of 468, 381, 388, 407, 413 ps. What is the global skew of the tree, in ps?
problems.e: Global skew is the largest latency minus the smallest: 468 - 381 = 87 ps.

problems.q: After CTS, the 4 clock sinks of a block report latencies of 462, 443, 459, 403 ps. What is the global skew of the tree, in ps?
problems.e: Global skew is the largest latency minus the smallest: 462 - 403 = 59 ps.

problems.q: After CTS, the 8 clock sinks of a block report latencies of 445, 430, 456, 430, 423, 406, 462, 425 ps. What is the global skew of the tree, in ps?
problems.e: Global skew is the largest latency minus the smallest: 462 - 406 = 56 ps.

problems.q: Five flops have clock latencies (in ps) A = 469, B = 418, C = 407, D = 382, E = 390. Timing paths exist only from D to B, E to B, E to C. What is the worst local skew, the largest absolute latency difference over flop pairs joined by a timing path, in ps?
problems.e: Only sequentially adjacent pairs matter for timing. The largest difference over the three connected pairs is 36 ps, while the global skew over all five flops would be 87 ps.

problems.q: Five flops have clock latencies (in ps) A = 416, B = 406, C = 403, D = 441, E = 432. Timing paths exist only from E to C, C to E, C to D. What is the worst local skew, the largest absolute latency difference over flop pairs joined by a timing path, in ps?
problems.e: Only sequentially adjacent pairs matter for timing. The largest difference over the three connected pairs is 38 ps, while the global skew over all five flops would be 38 ps.

problems.q: Five flops have clock latencies (in ps) A = 403, B = 437, C = 436, D = 450, E = 402. Timing paths exist only from C to A, C to D, D to E. What is the worst local skew, the largest absolute latency difference over flop pairs joined by a timing path, in ps?
problems.e: Only sequentially adjacent pairs matter for timing. The largest difference over the three connected pairs is 48 ps, while the global skew over all five flops would be 48 ps.

label: Clock slew and the transition limit
lesson:
# Clock slew and the transition limit

Clock edges must be sharp. A slow clock transition makes flop timing unpredictable, increases short-circuit power in every clock pin and makes the tree more sensitive to noise and variation. Libraries and design rules therefore impose a maximum transition (slew) on clock nets, usually tighter than on data nets. The slew limit is what forces a CTS engine to insert buffers at all: it caps how much capacitance and wire one driver may see.

## The single-pole estimate

Model a buffer driving a lumped load as a resistance $R$ charging a capacitance $C$. The output is $v(t) = V(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ with $\tau = RC$. It crosses 10% of the swing at $t_{10} = \tau \ln(10/9)$ and 90% at $t_{90} = \tau \ln 10$, so the 10-90% transition time is
$$t_{10\text{-}90} = \tau \ln 9 \approx 2.197\,RC.$$
For $R = 700\ \Omega$ and $C = 70$ fF, $RC = 49\,000\ \Omega\cdot$fF $= 49$ ps and the slew is about 107.7 ps. The estimate ignores the nonlinear driver and the wire's distributed resistance, but it is the right first-order tool for sizing and fanout decisions.

## Maximum load for a slew limit

Invert the estimate. A limit $S$ allows at most $C_{max} = S/(R \ln 9)$. With $S = 150$ ps and $R = 350\ \Omega$, $C_{max} = 150\,000/(2.197 \cdot 350) = 195.1$ fF. In a library this is what the max_capacitance and max_transition attributes encode for each cell, and CTS reads them as hard constraints. Remember the unit bookkeeping: ohms times femtofarads give femtoseconds, so divide by 1000 for picoseconds.

## From load budget to fanout

Each sink costs its clock-pin capacitance plus a share of wire. If a buffer of $650\ \Omega$ must meet 110 ps, its budget is $110\,000/(2.197 \cdot 650) = 77.0$ fF; at 2.5 fF of pin and 4 fF of wire per sink it can drive $\lfloor 77.0/6.5 \rfloor = 11$ sinks. That number, the maximum fanout, sets how wide each tree level can be and so how many levels the tree needs. Stronger buffers (lower $R$) raise the fanout but present more input capacitance to the stage above, which is the trade-off that logical effort makes precise.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits: A Design Perspective" (2nd ed., 2003), chapters on delay and interconnect; the Liberty reference manual's descriptions of max_transition and max_capacitance.

problems.q: A clock buffer with an output resistance of $200\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load of 100 fF. Treating the stage as a single RC pole, what is the 10-90% output transition time, in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A single pole crosses 10% at $\tau\ln(10/9)$ and 90% at $\tau\ln 10$, so the 10-90 time is $\tau\ln 9 = 2.197\,RC$. With $RC = 200 \cdot 100$ ohm-fF $= 20$ ps the slew is 43.9 ps.

problems.q: A clock buffer with an output resistance of $600\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load of 230 fF. Treating the stage as a single RC pole, what is the 10-90% output transition time, in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A single pole crosses 10% at $\tau\ln(10/9)$ and 90% at $\tau\ln 10$, so the 10-90 time is $\tau\ln 9 = 2.197\,RC$. With $RC = 600 \cdot 230$ ohm-fF $= 138$ ps the slew is 303.2 ps.

problems.q: A clock buffer with an output resistance of $300\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load of 80 fF. Treating the stage as a single RC pole, what is the 10-90% output transition time, in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A single pole crosses 10% at $\tau\ln(10/9)$ and 90% at $\tau\ln 10$, so the 10-90 time is $\tau\ln 9 = 2.197\,RC$. With $RC = 300 \cdot 80$ ohm-fF $= 24$ ps the slew is 52.7 ps.

problems.q: The clock transition limit is 70 ps. A buffer with output resistance $500\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load. Using the single-pole estimate (10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$), what is the largest load it may drive, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.

The clock transition limit is 80 ps. A buffer with output resistance $500\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load. Using the single-pole estimate (10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$), what is the largest load it may drive, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.

The clock transition limit is 90 ps. A buffer with output resistance $800\ \Omega$ drives a lumped load. Using the single-pole estimate (10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$), what is the largest load it may drive, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.

A clock buffer has output resistance $450\ \Omega$ and the transition limit is 130 ps (single-pole estimate, 10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$). Each sink adds 3 fF of clock-pin capacitance and 3 fF of wire. How many sinks can the buffer drive without violating the limit?
problems.e: The largest load is $130000/(2.197\cdot450)$ = 131.48 fF. Each sink costs 6 fF, so $\lfloor 131.48 / 6 \rfloor = 21$ sinks.

problems.q: A clock buffer has output resistance $750\ \Omega$ and the transition limit is 140 ps (single-pole estimate, 10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$). Each sink adds 2.5 fF of clock-pin capacitance and 1.5 fF of wire. How many sinks can the buffer drive without violating the limit?
problems.e: The largest load is $140000/(2.197\cdot750)$ = 84.96 fF. Each sink costs 4 fF, so $\lfloor 84.96 / 4 \rfloor = 21$ sinks.

problems.q: A clock buffer has output resistance $600\ \Omega$ and the transition limit is 120 ps (single-pole estimate, 10-90% time $= RC\ln 9$). Each sink adds 3 fF of clock-pin capacitance and 3 fF of wire. How many sinks can the buffer drive without violating the limit?
problems.e: The largest load is $120000/(2.197\cdot600)$ = 91.02 fF. Each sink costs 6 fF, so $\lfloor 91.02 / 6 \rfloor = 15$ sinks.

label: Clock network power
lesson:
# Clock network power

The clock is the busiest net on a chip: it toggles every cycle, reaches every flop and carries the longest wires. In many designs the clock network is a large share of dynamic power, often cited as a third or more. Every CTS decision, from topology to buffer count, is also a power decision, and clock gating exists because of this term. A tool designer needs the clock-power formula at their fingertips to judge any proposed network.

## Activity one

Dynamic power is $P = \alpha C V^2 f$, where $\alpha$ is the probability of a 0-to-1 transition per cycle, $C$ the switched capacitance, $V$ the supply and $f$ the clock frequency. A clock rises once every cycle, so $\alpha = 1$ and $P = C V^2 f$. The units work out neatly: picofarads times volts squared times gigahertz give milliwatts. A network of 200 pF at 0.8 V and 2 GHz burns $200 \cdot 0.64 \cdot 2 = 256$ mW. That is why clock capacitance is a first-class objective in CTS, next to skew.

## Where the capacitance lives

Clock capacitance has three parts: wire, sink pins and the buffers themselves. A tree with 120 mm of wire at 0.21 pF/mm, 21 000 flop pins of 0.8 fF and 330 buffers of 2 fF switched capacitance has $25.2 + 16.8 + 0.66 = 42.66$ pF. At 0.75 GHz and 0.95 V this is 28.9 mW. The breakdown tells the designer where to act: wire capacitance responds to topology and wirelength, pin capacitance only to gating, and buffer capacitance to sizing and stage count. A mesh, for example, attacks skew by adding wire and so pays mostly in the first term.

## The clock's share of total power

Data nets switch less often. With 240 pF of clock at activity 1 and 750 pF of data at average activity 0.12, the effective switched capacitances are 240 and 90 pF; the common factor $V^2 f$ cancels, so the clock takes $240/330 = 72.7\%$ of dynamic power. Shares like this explain the economics of clock gating: removing clock toggles from idle registers attacks the largest term. Activity factors for data come from simulation or from probabilistic propagation, which the power-analysis concepts cover.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits: A Design Perspective" (2nd ed., 2003), the chapter on power; Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

problems.q: A clock network has 60 pF of total switched capacitance and runs at 1.5 GHz from a 0.75 V supply. What is its dynamic power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A clock makes one rising transition every cycle, so its activity factor is 1: $P = C V^2 f = 60 \cdot 0.75^2 \cdot 1.5 = 50.6$ mW (pF times V squared times GHz gives mW).

problems.q: A clock network has 390 pF of total switched capacitance and runs at 1.5 GHz from a 0.8 V supply. What is its dynamic power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A clock makes one rising transition every cycle, so its activity factor is 1: $P = C V^2 f = 390 \cdot 0.8^2 \cdot 1.5 = 374.4$ mW (pF times V squared times GHz gives mW).

problems.q: A clock network has 230 pF of total switched capacitance and runs at 0.75 GHz from a 0.65 V supply. What is its dynamic power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: A clock makes one rising transition every cycle, so its activity factor is 1: $P = C V^2 f = 230 \cdot 0.65^2 \cdot 0.75 = 72.9$ mW (pF times V squared times GHz gives mW).

problems.q: A clock tree has 100 mm of wire at 0.25 pF/mm, drives 33000 flop clock pins of 0.5 fF each, and contains 150 buffers whose switched capacitance is 4 fF each. At 2.75 GHz and 0.6 V, what is the clock power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Total capacitance: 25 pF of wire + 16.5 pF of pins + 0.6 pF of buffers = 42.1 pF. Then $P = CV^2f = 41.7$ mW.

problems.q: A clock tree has 240 mm of wire at 0.24 pF/mm, drives 35000 flop clock pins of 0.7 fF each, and contains 170 buffers whose switched capacitance is 4 fF each. At 3 GHz and 0.9 V, what is the clock power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Total capacitance: 57.6 pF of wire + 24.5 pF of pins + 0.68 pF of buffers = 82.78 pF. Then $P = CV^2f = 201.2$ mW.

problems.q: A clock tree has 75 mm of wire at 0.23 pF/mm, drives 14000 flop clock pins of 0.7 fF each, and contains 160 buffers whose switched capacitance is 3 fF each. At 2.25 GHz and 0.95 V, what is the clock power, in mW? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Total capacitance: 17.25 pF of wire + 9.8 pF of pins + 0.48 pF of buffers = 27.53 pF. Then $P = CV^2f = 55.9$ mW.

problems.q: A design switches 90 pF of clock capacitance (activity 1) and 400 pF of data capacitance with an average activity factor of 0.05 (0-to-1 transitions per cycle). What share of the dynamic power does the clock take, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $V^2 f$ is common to both and cancels. Clock: 90 pF. Data: $0.05 \cdot 400 = 20$ pF effective. Share = 90 / 110 = 81.8%.

problems.q: A design switches 250 pF of clock capacitance (activity 1) and 700 pF of data capacitance with an average activity factor of 0.13 (0-to-1 transitions per cycle). What share of the dynamic power does the clock take, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $V^2 f$ is common to both and cancels. Clock: 250 pF. Data: $0.13 \cdot 700 = 91$ pF effective. Share = 250 / 341 = 73.3%.

problems.q: A design switches 230 pF of clock capacitance (activity 1) and 250 pF of data capacitance with an average activity factor of 0.08 (0-to-1 transitions per cycle). What share of the dynamic power does the clock take, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $V^2 f$ is common to both and cancels. Clock: 230 pF. Data: $0.08 \cdot 250 = 20$ pF effective. Share = 230 / 250 = 92%.

label: H-trees
lesson:
# H-trees

The H-tree is the classic symmetric clock topology: an H whose four tips each feed a smaller H, recursively. Because every root-to-sink path has the same shape, nominal skew is zero for uniformly distributed sinks. H-trees are still used for the top level of clock distribution in high-performance designs, and OpenROAD's CTS builds H-tree-style topologies over sink clusters. The geometry also gives clean closed forms for wirelength, which make it a good reference point for any other network.

## The recursive geometry

Take a square die of side $D$. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ through the centre, and two vertical bars of length $D/2$ at its ends, so its total length is $1.5D$ and its four tips are the centres of the four quadrants. Each tip is the centre of a level-2 H of half the size, total $0.75D$, and so on. After $n$ levels there are $4^n$ tips, each the centre of a cell of side $D/2^n$, which is where the sinks or the next stage of distribution attach.

## Wirelength level by level

Level $k$ has $4^{k-1}$ H's, each of length $1.5D/2^{k-1}$, so the level's total is $1.5D \cdot 2^{k-1}$: wirelength doubles every level, because the count quadruples while the size halves. Summing the geometric series over $n$ levels gives $1.5D(2^n - 1)$. For $D = 8000$ µm and $n = 2$ that is $1.5 \cdot 8000 \cdot 3 = 36\,000$ µm; level 4 alone of a 9000 µm H-tree is $1.5 \cdot 9000 \cdot 8 = 108\,000$ µm. The doubling tells you that the bottom levels dominate wire and power, which is why the last levels are often replaced by local trees.

## Equal path length and its limits

Within a level-$k$ H, a path runs half a horizontal bar and half a vertical bar, $D/2^{k+1} + D/2^{k+1} = D/2^k$. Over $n$ levels every source-to-sink path has length $D(1 - 2^{-n})$, so for $D = 10\,000$ µm and four levels each path is 9375 µm. Equal length gives zero nominal skew, but only nominally: real sinks are not uniform, loads differ, blockages force detours, and process variation affects each branch differently. That is why H-trees are tuned, combined with meshes, or replaced by algorithms such as DME that adapt to the actual sink locations.

## Going deeper

Bakoglu, "Circuits, Interconnections, and Packaging for VLSI" (1990), the chapter on clock distribution; the OpenROAD documentation for the CTS module.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 8000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. What is the total wirelength of all the level-3 H's together, in µm?
problems.e: Level 3 has $4^{2} = 16$ H's, each $1.5D/2^{2}$ long. The total is $1.5D\cdot 2^{2} = 48000$ µm: wirelength doubles every level because the count quadruples while the size halves.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 3000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. What is the total wirelength of all the level-4 H's together, in µm?
problems.e: Level 4 has $4^{3} = 64$ H's, each $1.5D/2^{3}$ long. The total is $1.5D\cdot 2^{3} = 36000$ µm: wirelength doubles every level because the count quadruples while the size halves.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 6000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. What is the total wirelength of all the level-5 H's together, in µm?
problems.e: Level 5 has $4^{4} = 256$ H's, each $1.5D/2^{4}$ long. The total is $1.5D\cdot 2^{4} = 144000$ µm: wirelength doubles every level because the count quadruples while the size halves.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 3000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. The tree has 3 levels and so drives $4^{3} = 64$ sinks. What is its total wirelength, in µm?
problems.e: Level $k$ contributes $1.5D\cdot2^{k-1}$. Summing the geometric series over $k = 1..3$ gives $1.5D(2^{3}-1) = 31500$ µm.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 9000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. The tree has 4 levels and so drives $4^{4} = 256$ sinks. What is its total wirelength, in µm?
problems.e: Level $k$ contributes $1.5D\cdot2^{k-1}$. Summing the geometric series over $k = 1..4$ gives $1.5D(2^{4}-1) = 202500$ µm.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 12000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. The tree has 4 levels and so drives $4^{4} = 256$ sinks. What is its total wirelength, in µm?
problems.e: Level $k$ contributes $1.5D\cdot2^{k-1}$. Summing the geometric series over $k = 1..4$ gives $1.5D(2^{4}-1) = 270000$ µm.

problems.q: An H-tree serves a square die of side $D = 12000$ µm. The level-1 H has a horizontal bar of length $D/2$ whose ends feed two vertical bars, each of length $D/2$. Each tip of a level-$k$ H is the centre of a level-$(k+1)$ H of half the size. The tree has 4 levels. What is the wire path length from the centre of the die to any one sink, in µm? Round to 1 decimal place.

Round to 1 decimal place.

label: Clock meshes
lesson:
# Clock meshes

A clock mesh is a grid of horizontal and vertical wires shorted together and driven at many points, usually by the leaves of a tree. Every sink connects to its nearest mesh wire with a short stub. Because the mesh has loops, each sink sees many parallel paths, which averages out driver mismatch and variation. Meshes give the lowest skew of any common topology, which is why high-performance processors use them, but they pay in wire, power and analysis effort.

## Mesh geometry and wirelength

A mesh over a $D \times D$ region with $m$ horizontal and $m$ vertical full-span wires has wirelength $2mD$. For a 3 mm square with 24 wires each way that is 144 mm, before counting the stubs to the sinks and the tree that drives the mesh. The mesh pitch $D/m$ sets how long the stubs are, and therefore how much residual skew the stubs add; a finer mesh lowers skew and raises wire. Unlike a tree, a mesh's wirelength does not depend on where the sinks are, which is both its robustness and its waste.

## The power cost

All of the mesh toggles every cycle. A 52 by 52 mesh over a 4 mm square at 0.28 pF/mm has $2 \cdot 52 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.28 = 116.5$ pF of wire; with 9000 pins of 1.2 fF it switches 127.3 pF, which at 3 GHz and 0.75 V is $127.3 \cdot 0.5625 \cdot 3 = 214.8$ mW. Mesh drivers also fight briefly whenever their input edges are skewed, adding short-circuit current. These costs are why meshes are reserved for the regions where skew matters most.

## Comparing a mesh with an H-tree

On the same region, a four-level H-tree uses $1.5D(2^4 - 1) = 22.5D$ of wire, so a mesh with 16 wires each way ($32D$) uses $9.5D$ more; at $D = 4$ mm and 0.24 pF/mm that is about 9.1 pF, which costs $9.1 V^2 f$ in extra power. The mesh buys lower skew and tolerance of variation, since a weak driver or a slow branch is compensated by its neighbours. The analysis cost is the other price: a mesh is not an RC tree, so Elmore's closed form does not apply, and its delays must come from solving the mesh as a linear circuit or from transient simulation.

## Going deeper

Restle et al., "A clock distribution network for microprocessors", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (2001); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

problems.q: A clock mesh covers a 3 mm by 3 mm region with 28 horizontal and 28 vertical wires, each spanning the full region. What is the mesh wirelength, in mm?
problems.e: Each direction has 28 wires of 3 mm: $2 \cdot 28 \cdot 3 = 168$ mm.

problems.q: A clock mesh covers a 3 mm by 3 mm region with 32 horizontal and 32 vertical wires, each spanning the full region. What is the mesh wirelength, in mm?
problems.e: Each direction has 32 wires of 3 mm: $2 \cdot 32 \cdot 3 = 192$ mm.

label: Spines, fishbones and hybrid clock networks
lesson:
# Spines, fishbones and hybrid clock networks

Real clock networks mix structures. A spine (or fishbone) is a wide, strongly driven trunk with short ribs to nearby sinks; a mesh shorts many branches together; a tree adapts to irregular sinks. Hybrid networks put a symmetric tree on top, a mesh or spines in the middle, and synthesised local trees at the bottom. Choosing the mix is a skew, power and robustness trade-off, and a CTS engine designer must know which parts are automated and which are structured by hand.

## Spines and fishbones

A spine is one or a few low-resistance trunks running across a region, driven strongly from one or both ends or from a tree. Ribs branch off at right angles to reach the sinks, and because each rib is short its delay is small. The skew is then set mainly by position along the spine, which a wide, low-resistance trunk keeps small. Spines suit row-structured or datapath regions where sinks line up. Compared with a mesh they use less wire, since there is no redundant cross-connection, but they average out less variation.

## Choosing among tree, mesh and spine

The trade-offs line up roughly like this. A synthesised tree uses the least wire and power and adapts to any sink distribution, but variation between its branches is uncorrelated, so its skew degrades in silicon. A mesh gives the lowest and most robust skew but burns the most power and needs circuit-level analysis. A spine sits between them. A sensible design spends power where skew matters: a mesh or spine over a dense, high-frequency core, and ordinary trees for scattered or slower logic. A pure H-tree fits uniform sinks; uneven placement wastes its wire.

## Hybrid and multi-source distribution

In a hybrid network a global H-tree drives many mesh or spine drivers with low skew, the mesh shorts out what remains, and short stubs or local trees reach the flops. **Multi-source CTS** formalises the bottom split: a structured top level delivers the clock to many tap points across the die, and an ordinary CTS builds a small tree from each tap to its nearby sinks. Two consequences matter to tool builders. The tree feeding a mesh must itself have low skew, or mesh drivers fight and waste current. And any structure with loops must be analysed as a circuit, not with tree formulas.

## Going deeper

Restle et al., "A clock distribution network for microprocessors", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (2001); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

problems.q:
Which description fits a clock spine (fishbone) network?

A) A full two-dimensional grid of shorted wires driven at many points

B) A recursive H shape whose every sink is at the same path length

C) A separate buffered tree for every flop

D) One or a few wide trunks across the die, with short branches (ribs) tapping off to nearby sinks
problems.a: One or a few wide trunks across the die, with short branches (ribs) tapping off to nearby sinks
problems.e: A spine is a low-resistance trunk driven strongly; ribs are short, so the skew a rib adds is small and set mostly by the position along the spine.

problems.q:
What does multi-source CTS mean?

A) Several PLLs drive the same flop

B) The clock is generated by many independent oscillators

C) Each sink receives two clocks and chooses the earlier

D) A top-level tree or mesh drives many tap points across the die, and an ordinary CTS builds a small tree from each tap to nearby sinks
problems.a: A top-level tree or mesh drives many tap points across the die, and an ordinary CTS builds a small tree from each tap to nearby sinks
problems.e: It splits the problem: a structured, hand-tuned top level for low skew across the die, and automated local trees whose short span keeps their skew small.

problems.q:
A hybrid clock network on a high-performance processor typically combines which pieces?

A) Two independent meshes at different frequencies

B) Only local trees, with no global structure

C) A spine driving the H-tree that drives the PLL

D) A global H-tree or balanced tree that drives a mesh, from which short local trees or stubs reach the flops
problems.a: A global H-tree or balanced tree that drives a mesh, from which short local trees or stubs reach the flops
problems.e: The tree delivers the edge to many mesh drivers with low skew, the mesh shorts out residual skew, and local stubs keep the last-level load small.

problems.q:
A team moves from a clock tree to a clock mesh. Which pair of effects should they expect?

A) Lower skew and lower power

B) Lower skew and better tolerance of variation, but noticeably higher clock power and wiring

C) No change in skew, lower wiring

D) Higher skew but lower power
problems.a: Lower skew and better tolerance of variation, but noticeably higher clock power and wiring
problems.e: The mesh's redundant wire adds capacitance that toggles every cycle; that is the price of shorting out mismatch.

problems.q:
A team moves from a clock tree to a clock mesh. Which pair of effects should they expect?

A) Higher skew but lower power

B) Lower skew and lower power

C) No change in skew, lower wiring

D) Lower skew and better tolerance of variation, but noticeably higher clock power and wiring
problems.a: Lower skew and better tolerance of variation, but noticeably higher clock power and wiring
problems.e: The mesh's redundant wire adds capacitance that toggles every cycle; that is the price of shorting out mismatch.

problems.q:
Why does an H-tree's zero nominal skew not survive into silicon unchanged?

A) Skew is undefined for symmetric trees

B) Its path lengths are unequal by construction

C) H-trees cannot be buffered

D) Process variation, uneven sink loads and blockages make the nominally equal branches differ
problems.a: Process variation, uneven sink loads and blockages make the nominally equal branches differ
problems.e: Symmetry equalises geometry, not physics. Real sinks are not uniform and real wires vary, so the tree needs tuning or a mesh to absorb the differences.

problems.q:
Mesh drivers are fed by a tree, and two adjacent drivers receive their input edges at different times. What does the mesh do?

A) The drivers fight briefly through the mesh, causing short-circuit current until both switch, while the mesh output edge is averaged

B) Nothing, because mesh drivers never overlap

C) The later driver is disabled automatically

D) The mesh holds the earlier edge forever
problems.a: The drivers fight briefly through the mesh, causing short-circuit current until both switch, while the mesh output edge is averaged
problems.e: Driver input skew turns into contention current and extra power, which is why the tree feeding a mesh must itself have low skew.

problems.q:
In a mesh driven by many buffers, one driver is much weaker than its neighbours. What happens?

A) The whole mesh stops toggling

B) Neighbouring drivers supply its region through the mesh, so the local skew penalty is small

C) Its sinks see a doubled frequency

D) Its region loses the clock entirely
problems.a: Neighbouring drivers supply its region through the mesh, so the local skew penalty is small
problems.e: Shorting is the point of a mesh: drive is shared, so one weak driver is partially compensated by the others.

problems.q:
Why cannot a standard timer simply apply Elmore delay to a clock mesh?

A) The mesh's delay is always zero

B) Meshes have no resistance

C) Elmore delay is only defined for inverters

D) Elmore's closed form needs an RC tree; a mesh has loops, so delays need a circuit solve over the whole mesh
problems.a: Elmore's closed form needs an RC tree; a mesh has loops, so delays need a circuit solve over the whole mesh
problems.e: The shared-resistance formula depends on unique root-to-node paths. With loops, mesh analysis needs a linear-system or transient simulation.

label: Skew of a given clock tree
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Skew of a given clock tree

Before building trees, a CTS engine must evaluate them. Given a candidate topology with wire resistances and capacitances, it computes the delay to every sink and the skew. Elmore delay is the standard first estimate, cheap enough to call inside every merge and every move. This concept applies Elmore delay to clock trees and introduces the simplest skew repair, a dummy load at the faster sink, which shows how capacitance moves delay.

## Elmore delay at a clock sink

In an RC tree, the Elmore delay to a node is the sum over edges on its root path of the edge resistance times the capacitance downstream of that edge. Compute downstream capacitance bottom-up first. Take a root that drives node u through $100\ \Omega$ ($C_u = 10$ fF) and node w through $150\ \Omega$ ($C_w = 20$ fF); u feeds sinks of 30 and 20 fF through $100\ \Omega$ each, and w feeds a 30 fF sink through $400\ \Omega$. Downstream of w is 50 fF, so the delay to w's sink is $150 \cdot 50 + 400 \cdot 30 = 19\,500\ \Omega\cdot$fF, which is 19.5 ps.

## Skew from the sink delays

Repeat the computation for every sink and subtract the smallest delay from the largest. In a tree where u carries 60 fF and w carries 20 fF, sinks might sit at 7, 14 and 4 ps, giving a skew of 10 ps. Two effects drive the imbalance: a sink at the end of a long or resistive branch, and a heavy sibling that loads the shared edge above it. A timer computes all sink delays in one pre-order pass after one post-order pass, so the cost is linear in the tree size. CTS engines evaluate thousands of candidate trees this way.

## Balancing with a dummy load

Adding capacitance $\Delta C$ at a sink slows every node above it. With a trunk $R_0$ and two branches $R_a$ and $R_b$, a load at sink b raises both sinks' delay by $R_0 \Delta C$ through the shared trunk, and sink b's by a further $R_b \Delta C$. The skew therefore closes by $R_b \Delta C$, so a 5 ps skew with $R_b = 200\ \Omega$ needs $\Delta C = 5000/200 = 25$ fF at the faster sink. Dummy loads are cheap to add but cost power and latency. CTS engines usually prefer to re-balance through tapping points, wire snaking or buffer sizing.

## Going deeper

Elmore, "The transient response of damped linear networks with particular regard to wideband amplifiers", Journal of Applied Physics (1948); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

problems.q: A clock driver feeds a trunk of $400\ \Omega$ into node t ($C_t = 5$ fF). Branch a ($200\ \Omega$) ends at sink a with 40 fF; branch b ($400\ \Omega$) ends at sink b with 10 fF. label: Zero-skew merging under linear delay
prereqs: Skew of a given clock tree
lesson:
# Zero-skew merging under linear delay

Zero-skew clock routing builds a tree bottom-up by merging pairs of subtrees, each already balanced, so that the merged tree is balanced too. The basic operation is choosing the tapping point on the wire between two subtree roots. Under the linear (path-length) delay model, where delay equals wire length, the choice is a one-line formula. It is the model behind DME's geometry and the right place to learn the merge before adding Elmore loading.

## Balancing the two sides

Let subtree 1 have delay $t_1$ from its root to every one of its sinks and subtree 2 have $t_2$, with the roots a wire of length $L$ apart. A tap at distance $x$ from root 1 sees delay $x + t_1$ to subtree 1's sinks and $(L - x) + t_2$ to subtree 2's. Zero skew requires these to be equal:
$$x = \frac{L + t_2 - t_1}{2}.$$
With $t_1 = 150$, $t_2 = 0$ and $L = 480$ µm, the tap is $(480 - 150)/2 = 165$ µm from subtree 1. The tap moves toward the slower subtree, so less new wire is added to the path that is already long.

## The merged delay

After the merge, the new subtree is again balanced, with delay $x + t_1 = (L + t_1 + t_2)/2$ from the tap to every sink. For $t_1 = 60$, $t_2 = 100$ and $L = 120$ µm, $x = 80$ µm and the merged delay is 140 µm. This value becomes the $t$ of the merged node when it is merged again higher up, so a whole tree is built by repeating the operation along a topology. The total wire added by a merge is exactly $L$ when the tap falls on the segment, which is why linear-delay zero-skew trees need no wire beyond the merge distances.

## When the tap leaves the segment

If $|t_1 - t_2| > L$, the formula gives $x < 0$ or $x > L$: even a tap at the faster subtree's root cannot equalise. The tap is then placed at the root of the slower subtree, and the wire to the faster subtree is elongated to length $|t_1 - t_2|$, by snaking. With $t_1 = 330$, $t_2 = 80$ and $L = 160$ µm, the wire must be 250 µm, so 90 µm of detour is added. Detour wire is pure waste in wirelength and power, so good topologies pair subtrees of similar delay, and bounded-skew methods relax the balance to avoid snaking.

## Going deeper

Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter; Chao, Hsu, Ho, Boese and Kahng, "Zero skew clock routing with minimum wirelength", IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems II (1992).

label: Tsay's zero-skew tapping point
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
Skew of a given clock tree
lesson:
# Tsay's zero-skew tapping point

Path length ignores how the downstream load slows a wire. Tsay's method keeps the bottom-up zero-skew merge but uses Elmore delay, so each subtree is summarised by its delay and its total capacitance. The tapping point then follows from a closed-form equation that is exact under Elmore. Tsay's merge is the standard building block of zero-skew clock routers and shows how capacitance, not only length, moves the balance point.

## The tapping-point formula

Merge subtree 1 (delay $t_1$, load $C_1$) and subtree 2 ($t_2$, $C_2$) with a wire of length $L$, resistance $r$ and capacitance $c$ per unit length. Put the tap at fraction $x$ from subtree 1, and model each side of the wire as a $\pi$ segment. Setting $r xL(c xL/2 + C_1) + t_1$ equal to $r(1-x)L(c(1-x)L/2 + C_2) + t_2$, the quadratic terms cancel and
$$x = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) + rL(C_2 + cL/2)}{rL(cL + C_1 + C_2)}.$$
With $L = 200$ µm, $r = 0.1\ \Omega$/µm, $c = 0.14$ fF/µm, $C_1 = 75$, $C_2 = 25$ fF, $t_1 = 35$ and $t_2 = 36$ ps: the numerator is $1 + 20 \cdot 39/1000 = 1.78$ ps, the denominator $20 \cdot 128/1000 = 2.56$ ps, so $x = 0.695$.

## The merged node

The merged subtree has delay equal to either side's: with the numbers above, $xL = 139.1$ µm, and $t_1 + r\,xL\,(c\,xL/2 + C_1)/1000 = 35 + 13.91 \cdot 84.73/1000 = 36.18$ ps; the subtree-2 side gives the same 36.18 ps. Its capacitance is $C_1 + C_2 + cL = 128$ fF. These two numbers, delay and load, are all the next merge needs, so the method climbs the topology in one bottom-up pass. Note that the heavier subtree pulls the tap toward itself: a large $C_1$ makes the wire on side 1 expensive, so $x$ shrinks.

## Elongation under Elmore delay

If $t_2 - t_1 > rL(cL/2 + C_1)$, the formula gives $x > 1$: subtree 2 is too slow even with the tap at its root. The tap moves onto root 2 and the wire to subtree 1 is lengthened to $L'$ with $rL'(cL'/2 + C_1) = t_2 - t_1$, a quadratic $(rc/2)L'^2 + rC_1L' - (t_2 - t_1) = 0$ with delays converted to the same units. For $r = 0.15$, $c = 0.18$, $C_1 = 20$ fF and a 2 ps gap, $0.0135L'^2 + 3L' - 2000 = 0$ gives $L' = 289.5$ µm. The case $x < 0$ is symmetric. Because Elmore delay grows quadratically with length, elongation under Elmore needs less extra wire than the linear model would suggest for large gaps.

label: Merging segments in the Manhattan plane
lesson:
# Merging segments in the Manhattan plane

In a real layout, a merge point is not on a fixed wire between two roots. It can be anywhere that has the right rectilinear distance to both children. The set of such points is the merging segment, a diagonal line in the Manhattan plane. Merging segments are the data structure that lets DME defer the choice of tap and so minimise wire; computing them, and distances to them, is the geometric core of every zero-skew router.

## Edge lengths from the zero-skew condition

Take sinks a and b with downstream delays $t_a$ and $t_b$ (path-length model) and Manhattan distance $d = |x_a - x_b| + |y_a - y_b|$. With no detour, the edges to a and b have lengths $e_a + e_b = d$ and zero skew needs $e_a + t_a = e_b + t_b$, so
$$e_a = \frac{d + t_b - t_a}{2}.$$
For $a = (40, 30)$ with $t_a = 0$ and $b = (20, 0)$ with $t_b = 10$, $d = 50$ and $e_a = 30$ µm. This is the linear merge, but in the plane: the edge lengths are fixed, the location is not.

## The shape of the segment

A point $p$ with $|p - a| = e_a$ and $|p - b| = e_b$, where $e_a + e_b = d$, must lie in the bounding box of a and b, since only there does the Manhattan triangle inequality hold with equality. Inside the box, $|p - a| = e_a$ is a line of slope $\pm 1$, so the merging segment is a diagonal (a Manhattan arc), clipped by the box. For $a = (50, 30)$, $t_a = 15$, $b = (20, 20)$, $t_b = 20$: $d = 40$ and $e_a = 22.5$. The segment runs from $(37.5, 20)$ to $(27.5, 30)$, an x extent of 10 µm. It shrinks to a point when the box is a line or when $e_a$ or $e_b$ is zero.

## Distance from a point to a segment

In the top-down pass, a placed parent at $p$ must be connected to the nearest point of the child's segment. Along a straight segment, Manhattan distance to $p$ is a convex piecewise-linear function, so its minimum is at an endpoint or at a point level with $p$ in x or in y. For the segment from $(17.5, 20)$ to $(27.5, 10)$ and $p = (0, 30)$, the endpoints are at 27.5 and 47.5, and no interior point is level with $p$, so the distance is 27.5 µm. When $p$ lies diagonally off the segment, every point of it can be equidistant, and any choice is optimal.

## Going deeper

label: Clock tree topology generation
prereqs: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
lesson:
# Clock tree topology generation

Zero-skew merging needs a topology: which sinks and subtrees merge with which, in what order. The embedding algorithm (DME) is optimal for a given topology, but the best topology is a hard combinatorial problem, so practical tools use geometric heuristics. The two classic ones are top-down partitioning by the method of means and medians, and bottom-up greedy matching. Both aim to pair nearby sinks of similar delay, which keeps merges short and avoids detour wire.

## Greedy nearest-pair merging

The simplest bottom-up rule merges the closest pair of current subtrees first, measured by Manhattan distance, replaces them by their merge node, and repeats. For sinks at $(60, 34)$, $(11, 41)$, $(11, 15)$ and $(14, 31)$, the closest pair is $(11, 41)$ and $(14, 31)$ at distance $3 + 10 = 13$ µm, so they merge first. With a nearest-neighbour structure each step is fast, and the result follows the placement closely. Its weakness is myopia: an early short merge can leave two far-apart leftovers that must be joined by a long, expensive edge.

## Means and medians

The method of means and medians (MMM) works top-down. It splits the sink set at the median x coordinate into two equal halves, then splits each half at its median y, alternating directions, until single sinks remain; the root connects the centres of mass of the two halves. For x coordinates 2, 6, 15, 56, 58 and 60, the median is $(15 + 56)/2 = 35.5$, so three sinks go to each side. Equal halves give a balanced topology whose depth is $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$, which keeps latency and the number of merges per path uniform.

## Matching rounds

Recursive geometric matching builds one level at a time. In each round it pairs all current subtrees, for instance greedily by repeatedly taking the closest unmatched pair, then merges every pair at once. For sinks at $(18, 22)$, $(49, 37)$, $(6, 41)$ and $(15, 47)$, the closest pair is $(6, 41)$ and $(15, 47)$ at 15 µm, which forces the remaining pair at 46 µm, a total of 61 µm. A round halves the number of subtrees, so the topology is balanced. Minimum-cost perfect matching would do better than greedy per round, at higher cost. Either way the topology then goes to Tsay or DME for embedding.

## Going deeper

label: Deferred-merge embedding
prereqs: Merging segments in the Manhattan plane
Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Deferred-merge embedding

Deferred-merge embedding (DME) is the algorithm that turns a clock topology into a zero-skew tree with minimum wire. Instead of fixing each merge point as it goes, it records every valid location as a merging segment on the way up, then chooses actual points on the way down, where each choice can be made relative to an already placed parent. Under the linear delay model DME is optimal for the given topology, and with Elmore delay it is the basis of most zero-skew routers.

## The bottom-up phase

Process the topology in post-order. A sink's segment is its own location. For an internal node with children segments $ms_a$ and $ms_b$, compute their Manhattan distance $d$, then the edge lengths from the zero-skew condition, $e_a = (d + t_b - t_a)/2$ and $e_b = d - e_a$ (or Tsay's formula under Elmore delay). The node's merging segment is the set of points within $e_a$ of $ms_a$ and $e_b$ of $ms_b$, the intersection of two tilted rectangular regions, which is again a Manhattan arc. For sinks at $(50, 0)$ with $t_a = 25$ and $(20, 20)$ with $t_b = 35$, $d = 50$ and $e_a = 30$ µm. If $|t_a - t_b| > d$, one edge needs detour wire.

## The top-down phase

Process the topology in pre-order. Place the root at any point of its segment, or at the point nearest the clock source. For every child, place it at the point of its own segment nearest its placed parent. Because the parent's segment lies at exactly distance $e$ from the child's segment, that nearest point is at distance $e$, so the planned edge length is realised with no detour. For a child segment from $(45, 20)$ to $(35, 30)$ and a parent at $(-10, 30)$, the nearest point is $(35, 30)$, 45 µm away. Each step is a constant-size geometric computation, so both phases take linear time.

## What deferral buys

Choosing a tap point early, as a greedy bottom-up router does, commits to one location before knowing where the parent will be, and later edges pay for the mismatch. DME keeps all equally good locations until the parent is fixed, which is why it achieves the minimum total wirelength among zero-skew trees for that topology under path-length delay. It does not choose the topology, which remains a heuristic problem, and under Elmore delay or with buffers its optimality is no longer exact. Bounded-skew DME generalises segments to regions, trading a skew budget for less wire.

## Going deeper

label: Bounded-skew clock trees
lesson:
# Bounded-skew clock trees

Zero skew is stricter than timing needs. If the timer tolerates a skew budget $B$, a merge no longer needs one exact tapping point: any tap whose merged skew stays within $B$ will do. That freedom is spent on shorter wire and fewer detours. Bounded-skew trees generalise zero-skew merging by tracking each subtree's minimum and maximum sink delay and by replacing merging segments with merging regions.

## Delay ranges instead of one delay

A bounded-skew subtree is summarised by the interval $[a, b]$ of its sink delays from its root, with $b - a \le B$. Merge subtree 1 ($[a_1, b_1]$) and subtree 2 ($[a_2, b_2]$) on a wire of length $L$, with the tap at $x$ from root 1, under path-length delay. From the tap, the latest sink is at $\max(x + b_1, L - x + b_2)$ and the earliest at $\min(x + a_1, L - x + a_2)$. The merged skew is their difference. With subtree delays $[120, 135]$ and $[90, 100]$, $L = 360$ and $x = 80$, the latest sink is at 380 and the earliest at 200, a skew of 180 µm, far outside any reasonable bound.

## The feasible tapping interval

Requiring merged skew at most $B$ gives two binding inequalities, slow side 2 against fast side 1 and slow side 1 against fast side 2:
$$\frac{L + b_2 - a_1 - B}{2} \le x \le \frac{L + a_2 - b_1 + B}{2},$$
clamped to $[0, L]$. With $[100, 115]$, $[80, 105]$, $L = 140$ and $B = 30$, the lower end is $(140 + 105 - 100 - 30)/2 = 57.5$ µm. When not clamped, the interval's width is $B - \tfrac{1}{2}[(b_1 - a_1) + (b_2 - a_2)]$: each subtree's own skew uses up part of the budget. A zero-skew merge of zero-skew subtrees is the special case of width zero.

## Spending the freedom

In the plane, the feasible taps form a merging region rather than a segment, and bounded-skew DME keeps these regions bottom-up and embeds top-down as before, choosing points that shorten the parent's edge. With $B = 0$ the method reduces to zero-skew DME; with $B$ unbounded it approaches a minimum Steiner tree, which ignores skew. Practical CTS uses a budget derived from the timing constraints, since the same skew that saves wire is taken from setup or hold margins. The region representation is more complex than a segment, which is the price of the extra freedom.

## Going deeper

Cong, Kahng, Koh and Tsao, "Bounded-skew clock and Steiner routing", ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems (1998).

label: Buffer levels and fanout in a clock tree
lesson:
# Buffer levels and fanout in a clock tree

An unbuffered wire tree works only over short spans. A real clock tree is a fanout tree of buffers, each driving a bounded number of loads, with a root buffer at the top. The fanout limit comes from slew and load constraints, and it sets the depth of the tree, its buffer count and its latency. Choosing the fanout is the first trade-off a buffered CTS makes: shallow trees with slow stages, or deep trees with fast ones.

## Levels from fanout

If no buffer may drive more than $F$ loads, $L$ levels of buffers reach at most $F^L$ sinks, so a tree for $N$ sinks needs $L = \lceil \log_F N \rceil$ levels. For 8092 flops and $F = 6$, $6^5 = 7776 < 8092 \le 6^6 = 46\,656$, so six levels are needed. The level count matters beyond latency: every level adds a stage whose delay varies independently on each branch, so deep trees accumulate more uncorrelated on-chip variation between sinks.

## Counting buffers

Working up from the sinks, the bottom level needs $\lceil N/F \rceil$ buffers, the next $\lceil \lceil N/F \rceil / F \rceil$, and so on until one root remains. For 2549 flops and $F = 3$, the counts are 850, 284, 95, 32, 11, 4, 2, 1, a total of 1279 buffers. The total is close to $N/(F - 1)$, so halving the fanout from 6 to 3 roughly multiplies the buffer count by 2.5. Buffers are clock power: each toggles every cycle, so buffer count enters the power objective directly.

## The fanout that minimises latency

A buffer's delay grows with its load. Model a stage driving $F$ loads as $a + bF$ ps, where $a$ is its intrinsic delay and $b$ the cost per load. Latency is $\lceil \log_F N \rceil (a + bF)$. For $N = 1000$, $a = 10$ and $b = 6$: fanout 2 needs 10 levels at 22 ps (220 ps), fanout 4 needs 5 levels at 34 ps (170 ps), fanout 8 needs 4 levels at 58 ps (232 ps). The optimum sits at a moderate fanout, the same result logical effort gives for optimal buffer chains, where the best stage effort is around 4. The ceiling makes the curve jagged, so tools evaluate candidates rather than solve for $F$.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

Buffer levels and fanout in a clock tree

lesson:
# Slew-limited buffer spacing

How far can one clock buffer drive a wire before the edge degrades too much? The answer sets the spacing of buffers along long clock routes and the size of the clusters a CTS engine builds. It comes from combining the Elmore delay of a driver plus wire plus load with a slew estimate, then solving for the length that just meets the transition limit. The quadratic growth of wire delay with length is what makes buffering necessary at all.

## Elmore delay of a driven wire

A buffer with output resistance $R_b$ drives a wire of length $L$ (resistance $r$, capacitance $c$ per unit length) into a load $C_{in}$, the next buffer's input. Its Elmore delay to the far end is
$$T = R_b(cL + C_{in}) + rL\left(\frac{cL}{2} + C_{in}\right).$$
The driver charges all capacitance; the wire's own resistance charges half of its capacitance and all of the load. For $R_b = 400\ \Omega$, $r = 1.3\ \Omega$/µm, $c = 0.24$ fF/µm, $C_{in} = 7$ fF and $L = 450$ µm, $T = 400 \cdot 115 + 585 \cdot 61 = 81\,685\ \Omega\cdot$fF, or 81.69 ps.

## From delay to slew

A common first-order estimate treats the response as a single pole with time constant equal to the Elmore delay, so the 10-90% slew is about $\ln 9 \cdot T \approx 2.197\,T$. For a wire with $T = 43.2$ ps the slew estimate is 95 ps. Real waveforms at the end of a resistive wire are not single-pole, and signoff timers use better models (effective capacitance, waveform propagation), but the estimate is accurate enough for deciding where buffers go. Its advantage is that it is a closed form in $L$.

## Solving for the longest wire

Setting $\ln 9 \cdot T = S$ for a limit $S$ gives a quadratic in $L$:
$$\frac{rc}{2}L^2 + (R_b c + r C_{in})L + R_b C_{in} - \frac{S}{\ln 9} = 0,$$
with $S/\ln 9$ in the same units as the other terms. For $R_b = 350\ \Omega$, $r = 1.5$, $c = 0.18$, $C_{in} = 2.5$ fF and $S = 60$ ps, the coefficients are 0.135, 66.75 and $875 - 27\,307$, and the positive root is about 260 µm. Beyond that the buffer must be repeated. The $L^2$ term is why doubling a wire more than doubles its delay, and why long routes are cut into buffered stages.

## Going deeper

Bakoglu, "Circuits, Interconnections, and Packaging for VLSI" (1990), the chapter on interconnect delay and repeaters; Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022).

RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Duty-cycle distortion in clock buffer chains

A clock buffer rarely has equal rising and falling delays. Each stage shifts one edge more than the other, so the high pulse grows or shrinks a little, and a deep tree accumulates the error. Designs that use both clock edges, latches or half-cycle paths, or that specify minimum pulse widths, are sensitive to this duty-cycle distortion. It is one reason clock trees are often built from inverters rather than buffers.

## One stage at a time

Let a buffer delay its rising output by $t_{LH}$ and its falling output by $t_{HL}$. An input high pulse of width $W$ rises at 0 and falls at $W$; at the output it rises at $t_{LH}$ and falls at $W + t_{HL}$. The output high pulse is $W + (t_{HL} - t_{LH})$. With $t_{LH} = 58$ and $t_{HL} = 66$ ps, each buffer widens the high pulse by 8 ps, and seven buffers turn a 925 ps pulse into 981 ps. The error is systematic, so it adds linearly with depth rather than averaging out.

## Duty cycle at the output

The duty cycle is the high time over the period. A 2000 ps clock at 50% has a 1000 ps high pulse; seven buffers with $t_{HL} - t_{LH} = 7$ ps make it 1049 ps, a duty cycle of 52.45%. Half-cycle paths, which launch on one edge and capture on the other, lose exactly the corresponding time on one of the two half cycles. Static timing sees this when clocks are propagated through characterised rise and fall arcs, and minimum-pulse-width checks catch pulses that become too narrow.

## Why inverters cancel

An inverter turns a high pulse into a low pulse: input rising at 0 gives output falling at $t_{HL}$, input falling at $W$ gives output rising at $W + t_{LH}$, a low pulse of $W + t_{LH} - t_{HL}$. The next inverter turns it back into a high pulse of $W + t_{LH} - t_{HL} + t_{HL} - t_{LH} = W$. Each pair of identical inverters cancels exactly, so an even inverter chain preserves the duty cycle and an odd one leaves one stage's error. Six buffers with a 3 ps mismatch followed by nine inverters with $t_{LH} - t_{HL} = -4$ ps give $625 + 18 - 4 = 639$ ps. Mismatch between nominally identical inverters still remains in silicon.

## Going deeper

Friedman, "Clock distribution networks in synchronous digital integrated circuits", Proceedings of the IEEE (2001); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003).

problems.q: A 1850 ps clock enters a chain of 5 identical buffers with a high pulse of 925 ps. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 30 ps and a falling output by 33 ps. What is the width of the high pulse at the chain output, in ps?
problems.e: Each buffer delays the rising edge by 30 and the falling edge by 33, so the high pulse changes by $t_{HL} - t_{LH} = 3$ ps per stage. After 5 stages: $925 + 5(3) = 940$ ps.

problems.q: A 1150 ps clock enters a chain of 7 identical buffers with a high pulse of 575 ps. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 51 ps and a falling output by 44 ps. What is the width of the high pulse at the chain output, in ps?
problems.e: Each buffer delays the rising edge by 51 and the falling edge by 44, so the high pulse changes by $t_{HL} - t_{LH} = -7$ ps per stage. After 7 stages: $575 + 7(-7) = 526$ ps.

problems.q: A 850 ps clock enters a chain of 6 identical buffers with a high pulse of 425 ps. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 48 ps and a falling output by 56 ps. What is the width of the high pulse at the chain output, in ps?
problems.e: Each buffer delays the rising edge by 48 and the falling edge by 56, so the high pulse changes by $t_{HL} - t_{LH} = 8$ ps per stage. After 6 stages: $425 + 6(8) = 473$ ps.

problems.q: A 850 ps clock with a 50% duty cycle passes 9 identical buffers. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 59 ps and a falling output by 64 ps. What is the duty cycle at the output, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The high pulse becomes $425 + 9(64 - 59) = 470$ ps, so the duty cycle is $470/850 = 55.29\%$.

problems.q: A 950 ps clock with a 50% duty cycle passes 5 identical buffers. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 49 ps and a falling output by 48 ps. What is the duty cycle at the output, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The high pulse becomes $475 + 5(48 - 49) = 470$ ps, so the duty cycle is $470/950 = 49.47\%$.

problems.q: A 750 ps clock with a 50% duty cycle passes 10 identical buffers. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 26 ps and a falling output by 33 ps. What is the duty cycle at the output, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The high pulse becomes $375 + 10(33 - 26) = 445$ ps, so the duty cycle is $445/750 = 59.33\%$.

problems.q: A 1550 ps clock with a 775 ps high pulse passes 6 buffers and then 7 inverters. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 35 ps and a falling output by 42 ps. Each inverter has a rising-output delay of 20 ps and a falling-output delay of 27 ps. What is the width at the output of the pulse that began as the input's high pulse (it ends up low if the chain inverts), in ps?
problems.e: The buffers change the pulse by 6(7) = 42 ps. Inverters alternate which output edge is rising, so each consecutive pair cancels exactly. With 7 inverters, one is left over: it turns the high pulse into a low pulse whose width changes by $t_{LH} - t_{HL} = -7$ ps. The result is 810 ps.

problems.q: A 1350 ps clock with a 675 ps high pulse passes 5 buffers and then 3 inverters. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 44 ps and a falling output by 41 ps. Each inverter has a rising-output delay of 28 ps and a falling-output delay of 29 ps. What is the width at the output of the pulse that began as the input's high pulse (it ends up low if the chain inverts), in ps?
problems.e: The buffers change the pulse by 5(-3) = -15 ps. Inverters alternate which output edge is rising, so each consecutive pair cancels exactly. With 3 inverters, one is left over: it turns the high pulse into a low pulse whose width changes by $t_{LH} - t_{HL} = -1$ ps. The result is 659 ps.

problems.q: A 1500 ps clock with a 750 ps high pulse passes 4 buffers and then 6 inverters. Each clock buffer delays a rising output by 33 ps and a falling output by 35 ps. Each inverter has a rising-output delay of 39 ps and a falling-output delay of 31 ps. What is the width at the output of the pulse that began as the input's high pulse (it ends up low if the chain inverts), in ps?
problems.e: The buffers change the pulse by 4(2) = 8 ps. Inverters alternate which output edge is rising, so each consecutive pair cancels exactly. With 6 inverters, all pairs cancel, so the result is 758 ps.

label: Insertion-delay balancing across sinks
prereqs: Buffer levels and fanout in a clock tree
lesson:
# Insertion-delay balancing across sinks

Not every clock sink is a simple flop pin. Macros such as memories have their own internal clock trees, IO registers sit far from the core, and some sinks hang off generated clocks. CTS must balance the latency at the registers that actually exchange data, not only at the pins it sees. It does so by targeting a common latency and padding early groups with delay. Understanding this is necessary to read a CTS report and to set the engine's targets.

## Register-level latency

A macro's clock pin is not where its registers capture. A memory with 150 ps of internal insertion delay from its clock pin to its internal registers, whose pin sees 280 ps, has a register-level latency of 430 ps. If the core flops see 359 ps and the IO flops 298 ps, the register-level skew is $430 - 298 = 132$ ps; balancing pins alone would report $359 - 280 = 79$ ps and be wrong. CTS tools therefore accept an insertion-delay value for macro clock pins, often taken from the macro's timing model, and balance the sum.

## Padding early groups

The usual target is the largest register-level latency, since delay can only be added. A group at latency $l$ below a target $T^\ast$ with tolerance $\tau$ needs $\lceil (T^\ast - \tau - l)/d \rceil$ delay cells of delay $d$. With a target of 397 ps, a tolerance of 5 ps and 25 ps cells, a group at 251 ps needs $\lceil 141/25 \rceil = 6$ cells. In practice the padding goes high in the tree, where one inserted cell delays a whole subtree, rather than at each sink.

## The cost of balancing

Padding is not free. Every delay cell toggles each cycle and adds power. Every added stage is a new source of on-chip variation that is not shared with the other groups, so balanced nominal latency can still mean skew in silicon. For four groups at 369, 256, 258 and 368 ps with a 20 ps tolerance and 25 ps cells, eight cells are inserted. When the gap comes from one large macro, a better fix may be to move the macro's clock entry point, use a faster path to it, or exploit useful skew, so that the rest of the design is not slowed to the macro's latency.

## Going deeper

Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter; the OpenROAD documentation for the CTS module.

label: The clock tree synthesis flow in OpenROAD
lesson:
# The clock tree synthesis flow in OpenROAD

In an open-source flow, CTS is a sequence of steps around the clock_tree_synthesis command of OpenROAD's CTS module (TritonCTS). Knowing the sequence explains why timing changes after CTS, why hold is fixed then, and where clock nets get special routing. A tool designer should be able to say what each step consumes and produces, and what breaks if a step is skipped.

## Where CTS sits

CTS runs after global and detailed placement and pre-CTS optimisation, and before global and detailed routing. Before CTS the timer treats clocks as ideal: zero network latency, with set_clock_uncertainty standing in for the skew the tree will add. CTS needs the placed sink locations and a list of clock buffer cells it may use; in OpenROAD the user passes the buffer list and optionally a root buffer to clock_tree_synthesis. The output is a placed buffer tree for every clock net, which the router then treats as fixed, high-priority nets.

## Inside the CTS step

OpenROAD's CTS groups nearby sinks into clusters, builds a balanced, H-tree-style topology over the clusters, and inserts buffers chosen from the allowed list using characterised delay and slew. Clustering keeps the leaf nets short and the top-level problem small. After tree construction the flow repairs long clock wires, and legalises the inserted buffers, because CTS places them where the topology wants, possibly on occupied sites. Clock nets are often given non-default routing rules: wider wires and larger spacing, or shields, which lower resistance and crosstalk on nets that toggle every cycle.

## After CTS

Timing then switches to propagated clocks, so every register sees its real latency through the tree. Results change. If the built tree has 120 ps of skew between critical pairs where 50 ps of uncertainty was budgeted, paths that met timing before CTS can now fail. Hold is repaired now, by inserting delay on short paths, because hold depends on real skew. On-chip variation matters too: pairs whose clock paths split near the root have long non-common paths, which carry more uncorrelated variation and get less credit from CPPR. CTS quality is reported as latency, skew, buffer count and wirelength together.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation for the CTS module and the OpenROAD flow scripts; Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the clock chapter.

problems.q:
What must a user give OpenROAD's CTS so that it can insert buffers?

A) The detailed routing guides

B) A list of all false paths

C) The SPEF of the routed design

D) The list of clock buffer cells it may use (and optionally the root buffer)
problems.a: The list of clock buffer cells it may use (and optionally the root buffer)
problems.e: CTS characterises and chooses among the allowed buffers; options such as the buffer list and root buffer steer that choice.

A) pdngen

B) clock_tree_synthesis

C) detailed_route

D) global_placement
problems.a: clock_tree_synthesis
problems.e: clock_tree_synthesis invokes the CTS module (TritonCTS); pdngen builds the power grid and the others are placement and routing steps.

A) During logic synthesis, before mapping

B) Before floorplanning

D) After detailed routing and signoff
problems.a: After placement and pre-CTS optimisation, before signal routing
problems.e: CTS needs sink locations from placement, and its buffers and clock wires must be placed and routed before the signal nets fill the resources.

label: Useful skew
lesson:
# Useful skew

Zero skew is not the goal; meeting timing is. If a flop's incoming path is too long and its outgoing path has slack, delaying that flop's clock lends time from one path to the other. This deliberate skew is called useful skew. Each flop's clock arrival then lives in a feasible window bounded by the setup and hold constraints of its neighbouring paths. Computing that window is the local version of clock scheduling, and modern CTS engines implement the result as latency targets.

## Lending time to a failing path

Let flop F capture from A and launch to B, with the clock reaching A and B at time 0 and F at time $s$. The path A to F meets setup when $t_{cq} + d_{max} + t_{su} \le s + T$. With period 800 ps, $t_{cq} = 45$, $d_{max} = 736$ and $t_{su} = 33$ ps, setup fails at $s = 0$ by 14 ps, and it is met for $s \ge 45 + 736 + 33 - 800 = 14$ ps. A later capture clock moves the required time out by exactly $s$. Nothing about the logic changes: the time comes from the next stage.

## The upper bounds

The same $s$ delays every launch from F. Setup on F to B requires $s + t_{cq} + d_{max,FB} + t_{su} \le T$, so $s \le T - t_{cq} - d_{max,FB} - t_{su}$. Hold on A to F requires the earliest new data to arrive after F's clock plus hold: $t_{cq} + d_{min,AF} \ge s + t_h$, so $s \le t_{cq} + d_{min,AF} - t_h$. With $T = 550$, $t_{cq} = 51$, $t_{su} = 30$, $t_h = 26$, $d_{max,FB} = 354$ and $d_{min,AF} = 187$, the bounds are 115 and 212 ps, and the tighter, 115 ps, wins. Hold is the constraint people forget: pushing a capture clock later also makes short paths into it fail.

## The feasible window

A fourth constraint, hold on F to B, gives another lower bound: $s + t_{cq} + d_{min,FB} \ge t_h$. The window is then $[\max(\text{lower bounds}), \min(\text{upper bounds})]$. With lower bounds 16 and -46 and upper bounds 175 and 180 ps, the window is $[16, 175]$, 159 ps wide. An empty window means skew cannot fix this flop alone and the logic must change. A wide window gives CTS freedom: it can implement any value inside it, and robust schedules aim for the middle so that variation cannot push the arrival outside. Choosing all flops' arrivals together is the scheduling problem.

## Going deeper

Fishburn, "Clock skew optimization", IEEE Transactions on Computers (1990); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), the timing closure chapter.

With $s = 0$ the path A to F fails setup. What is the smallest $s$ that makes it meet setup, in ps?

label: Clock scheduling as difference constraints
lesson:
# Clock scheduling as difference constraints

Every setup and hold check between two flops bounds the difference of their clock arrival times. A whole design's clock schedule is therefore a system of difference constraints, which has a beautiful graph structure: feasibility is the absence of a negative cycle, and a feasible schedule comes from shortest paths. This is the formulation behind clock-scheduling engines and the reason useful skew can be computed exactly on large designs.

## Constraints as a graph

For a path from flop $i$ to flop $j$, setup gives $t_i - t_j \le T - t_{cq} - d_{max} - t_{su}$ and hold gives $t_j - t_i \le t_{cq} + d_{min} - t_h$. Each constraint $t_v - t_u \le w$ becomes an edge from $u$ to $v$ of weight $w$. Summing constraints around any cycle cancels every $t$, so a cycle of negative total weight is a contradiction. For three flops in a ring with longest delays 1070, 720 and 810 ps, $t_{cq} = 70$ and $t_{su} = 34$, the cycle weight at $T = 930$ ps is $3 \cdot 930 - 2912 = -122$ ps: no schedule meets setup.

## Shortest paths give a schedule

Add a virtual source with a zero-weight edge to every node and run Bellman-Ford. If no negative cycle exists, the distances $t_v = \mathrm{dist}(v)$ satisfy every constraint, because a shortest path obeys $\mathrm{dist}(v) \le \mathrm{dist}(u) + w$, which is exactly $t_v - t_u \le w$. For constraints $t_D - t_C \le 5$, $t_C - t_D \le 30$, $t_D - t_A \le -15$ and $t_C - t_A \le 20$, relaxation gives $t = (0, 0, 0, -15)$ for A to D. If an edge can still be relaxed after $n - 1$ rounds, there is a negative cycle and the period is infeasible.

## The minimum period

With setup constraints only, every cycle $C$ of flops needs $|C| \cdot T \ge \sum_{C}(t_{cq} + d_{max} + t_{su})$, so the minimum period is the maximum over cycles of the mean stage delay. For a ring with delays 780, 640 and 1100 ps, $t_{cq} = 45$ and $t_{su} = 36$, it is $2763/3 = 921$ ps, below the 1181 ps the slowest stage would need with zero skew. Skew redistributes time around a loop but cannot create it. Hold constraints add edges of the opposite direction, so in general the minimum period is found by searching on $T$ with a negative-cycle test, or as a maximum cycle ratio.

## Going deeper

Fishburn, "Clock skew optimization", IEEE Transactions on Computers (1990); Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms", the section on difference constraints and shortest paths.

label: Maximum-slack clock scheduling as a linear program
lesson:
# Maximum-slack clock scheduling as a linear program

Feasibility is not enough: a schedule that meets every constraint with zero margin breaks under the first bit of variation. Clock scheduling is therefore posed as a linear program that maximises the minimum slack over all setup and hold checks. The decision variables are the clock arrival times and the margin; the constraints are the difference constraints with the margin subtracted. The LP's structure makes it solvable at scale, and its solution becomes the latency targets that CTS must implement.

## The formulation

Variables: an arrival time $t_i$ for each flop and a margin $M$. Objective: maximise $M$. Constraints: for each path $i \to j$, $t_i - t_j \le T - S_{ij} - M$ for setup, with $S_{ij} = t_{cq} + d_{max} + t_{su}$, and $t_j - t_i \le H_{ij} - M$ for hold, with $H_{ij} = t_{cq} + d_{min} - t_h$. For fixed $M$ these are difference constraints, so the LP is a parametric shortest-path problem; for a ring of $n$ flops with setup only, summing gives $M^\ast = T - \sum S/n$. With stage requirements summing to 1314 ps over two flops and $T = 700$ ps, $M^\ast = 700 - 657 = 43$ ps.

## A two-flop loop with hold

Let A and B launch into each other and set $u = t_A - t_B$. Setup A to B and hold B to A both bound $u$ from above: $u \le P - M$ with $P = \min(T - S_{AB}, H_{BA})$. Setup B to A and hold A to B bound it from below: $-u \le Q - M$ with $Q = \min(T - S_{BA}, H_{AB})$. Adding the two gives $M \le (P + Q)/2$, reached at $u = (P - Q)/2$. With $P = -18$ and $Q = 96$ ps, the best margin is 39 ps at $t_A - t_B = -57$ ps: B's clock should arrive 57 ps after A's.

## From schedule to tree

The LP's output is a target arrival for every flop, typically expressed as offsets from a common latency. CTS then builds a tree whose sink latencies hit those targets, for example by giving sinks different required delays in the merge, or by inserting delay on chosen branches. Two cautions apply. The targets are only as good as the path delays used to compute them, and those delays change after CTS and routing, so scheduling is iterated. And large intentional skews add latency on some branches, which costs power and adds variation. Production tools therefore limit how far a schedule may move any flop.

## Going deeper

Fishburn, "Clock skew optimization", IEEE Transactions on Computers (1990); Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, "Introduction to Linear Optimization" (1997), for the LP background.

label: Clock gating
lesson:
# Clock gating

Clock gating stops the clock to registers that do not need to change, removing the largest term in dynamic power for idle logic. Synthesis inserts integrated clock-gating cells (ICGs) where a register bank holds its value under an enable; CTS then builds the tree through them; and STA checks a special timing arc on their enable. Gating is simple to state and easy to get wrong, because a gated clock that glitches corrupts state silently.

## The integrated clock gate

For positive-edge flops, an ICG contains a latch that is transparent while the clock is low, followed by an AND of the latched enable with the clock. While the clock is low the latch follows the enable; when the clock rises the latch closes and the AND passes either a full pulse or none. A test-enable input forces the gated clock on during scan shift. For flops that capture on the falling edge the polarity flips: a latch transparent while the clock is high and an OR, so the disabled clock rests high. Libraries supply the ICG as one characterised cell, so tools recognise it as a clock element with a known internal timing relationship.

## Why a bare AND gate glitches

Gate a clock with a plain AND and the output follows the enable while the clock is high. For an 800 ps clock high from 0 to 400 ps, an enable that rises at 20 ps produces a 380 ps pulse that starts late; an enable that falls at 150 ps produces a 150 ps runt pulse. A runt pulse may clock some flops and not others, or violate their minimum pulse width, corrupting state. The latch in the ICG removes the problem by sampling the enable only while the clock is low, so the enable may change at any time during the high phase without effect.

## Gating in the flow

Synthesis finds register banks whose next-state logic is a feedback multiplexer, load the input when the enable is true and keep the old value otherwise, and replaces the multiplexer with an ICG on the bank's clock. CTS treats the ICG as a node of the tree, balancing through it so gated and ungated sinks still meet the skew target. STA performs a clock-gating setup and hold check of the enable against the ICG's clock pin. Placement of the gate is a trade-off: near the root it stops more of the tree but sees an earlier clock and tightens enable timing; near the flops it eases timing but saves less. Gating lowers average power, not the worst cycle: many gates opening together still create a large current step.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), the chapter on power; Keating, Flynn, Aitken, Gibbons and Shi, "Low Power Methodology Manual" (2007).
